Project Title: Towards improved seasonal prediction of precipitation over the west U.S. and understanding of its predictability sources using NOAAs Seasonal Forecast System
Project Goal: The primary goal of this project is to improve seasonal prediction skill for precipitation over the west U.S. in the new NOAA's seasonal prediction system (SFS), and to advance our understanding of the underlying predictability sources.
Research Keywords: Coupled Models & Techniques, Data Assimilation and Ensembles, Reanalysis & Reforecasting
Associated Forecast Systems & Models: Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS), Unified Forecast System (UFS)
Project Description: Current prediction frameworks exhibit limited skill in forecasting winter precipitation variations across the western United States, creating critical challenges for resource management. This project addresses these shortcomings by comprehensively evaluating developmental baselines (Phases 1-3) of NOAA's emerging Seasonal Forecast System (SFS). The research team will isolate and investigate critical large-scale North Pacific circulation anomalies independent of ENSO, test upscale impacts of tropical intraseasonal variability, and analyze Arctic sea ice modulations. In the final stage, a specialized diagnostic benchmarking software tool will be delivered directly to the SFS development team to isolate model tracking errors and optimize predictive mechanics.
Project Benefits: Provide critical guidance for SFS development to improve seasonal prediction skills over the west U.S., benefit the climate research community by advancing the fundamental understanding of essential large-scale patterns, and support water and energy managers for drought preparedness andRelated policymaking.

Project Title: Will Improving Land States Benefit S2S Forecasts? Novel Assessments Using Realistic Land State Uncertainties and Strongly-Coupled Land-Atmosphere All-Sky Satellite Infrared Radiance Data Assimilation
Project Goal: The primary goal is to advance the Unified Forecast System (UFS) subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) predictions by characterizing potential skill improvements from refining the precision of current land surface initial conditions (LSICs) and improving those conditions through strongly-coupled land-atmosphere (SCLA) all-sky geostationary satellite infrared radiance (GeoIR) ensemble data assimilation (EnsDA)
Research Keywords: Coupled Models & Techniques, Data Assimilation and Ensembles, Reanalysis & Reforecasting
Associated Forecast Systems & Models: Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS), Unified Forecast System (UFS)
Project Description:
This project addresses critical knowledge gaps in land-atmosphere interactions and data assimilation for the NOAA UFS through two main objectives:
Assessing LSIC Influence: The team will investigate how refining "already realistic" operational land state analyses impacts S2S forecast skill. This involve conducting global UFS S2S ensemble hindcast sensitivity experiments (up to 30-day lead time) for the boreal summer, focusing on how reduced land and atmospheric initial condition (IC) uncertainties propagate into forecast uncertainties.
Innovative Data Assimilation: The project will develop and test a new capability within the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) framework for SCLA all-sky GeoIR EnsDA. Using both imperfect model Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) and real data Observing System Experiments (OSEs), the researchers will evaluate how assimilating cloud-affected infrared observations (specifically the 6.2 m water vapor channel) can improve land surface initial states and subsequent S2S forecasts.
Project Benefits: Improved Operational Guidance on land surface observation investments, enhanced forecast skill for critical moisture/temperature metrics, and targeted workforce pipeline development to ease shortages in ensemble data assimilation fields.

Project Title: Improving NOAA UFS subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) prediction via implementing data assimilation of vegetation characteristics in JEDI and enhanced plant hydraulics physics
Project Goal: The primary goal is to improve the United Forecast System (UFS) subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) prediction skill by enhancing the representation of land-atmosphere interactions. This is achieved through the implementation of a Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI)-based land data assimilation (DA) system for vegetation characteristics and the integration of an advanced plant hydraulics (PH) module into the Noah-MP land surface model within the UFS.
Research Keywords: Coupled Models & Techniques, Data Assimilation and Ensembles
Project Description: This project implements two major structural updates to advance land surface modeling and coupled data assimilation within the NOAA UFS framework. First, a data assimilation capability will be developed within the JEDI system to assimilate satellite-derived vegetation products, including Leaf Area Index (LAI) and Vegetation Optical Depth (VOD), ensuring model vegetation metrics track consistently with real-time observation changes. Second, traditional semi-empirical soil-resistance transpiration schemes will be replaced by a physically-based plant hydraulics module that explicitly captures water transport from the soil through roots and stems to leaves, providing a realistic simulation of transpiration dynamics and canopy water stress feedback structures under extreme drought conditions.
Project Benefits: Enhances S2S prediction accuracy for temperature, humidity, and precipitation variables by providing superior land surface boundary conditions, improves regional model handling of flash drought onset and intense heatwaves, and establishes a unified, community-portable data assimilation environment via JEDI integration.

Project Title: Know, Explore, Improve: Hypothesis-driven Development of the UFS
Project Goal: The primary goal is to identify sources of predictability for precipitation, temperature, and drought on subseasonal to seasonal (S2S) timescales, and to better understand and improve their representation in the Seasonal Forecast System version 1 (SFSv1).
Research Keywords: Coupled Models & Techniques, Reanalysis & Reforecasting, Teleconnections
Associated Forecast Systems & Models: Seasonal Forecast System (SFS), Unified Forecast System (UFS)
Project Description: This project tests the hypothesis that systematic errors in key low-frequency climate modes, such as ENSO and the MJO, drive downstream predictive failures for precipitation extremes across the contiguous United States within NOAA's Seasonal Forecast System (SFS). To isolate these mechanisms, the research team will execute hierarchical modeling configurations using an operational "Replay" capability to systematically constrain model grid points against observations. The core experiments include generating multiple 30-year SFS ensembles to index systematic drift away from baseline climatology, alongside performing focused reforecast reconstructions of prominent hydrometeorological disasters-including the 1993 Midwest Floods, the 2007 Southeast Drought, and the 2020-2023 Western Drought-to deliver target feedback parameters directly to the operational model suite.
Project Benefits: Provides crucial model feedback to improve seasonal climatology handling within emerging forecast versions, yields unique multi-decade public datasets for Earth system research teams, assists regional water resource management groups with structural drought preparation criteria, and actively constructs educational pipelines by training students from underrepresented communities to deploy and execute the UFS infrastructure.
Combined Keywords: Coupled Models & Techniques, Reanalysis & Reforecasting, Teleconnections

Project Title: Predictability of the Summer Precipitation Extremes in the Southern Great Plains through the Remote Effects of Snow Dynamics in the US West
Project Goal: The project aims to improve the United Forecast System's (UFS) subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) predictability of early summer precipitation extremes in the Southern Great Plains (SGP) by leveraging western U.S. spring snowpack dynamics and land memory feedback channels within an enhanced UFS/Noah-MP configuration.
Research Keywords: Coupled Models & Techniques, Data Assimilation and Ensembles
Project Description: This project addresses critical structural deficiencies within current land surface models, targeting systematic underestimations of snow water equivalent (SWE), inadequate soil hydrology tracking, and missing vegetation adaptation mechanics. The research team will isolate how initial spring snow conditions modulate local surface heating and downstream precipitation anomalies via mechanism analysis using historical snow, soil moisture, and atmospheric reanalysis datasets. To prevent persistent warm and dry model drift across the central United States, the team will update Noah-MP representations of snow-rain partitioning, subgrid soil hydraulics (including macropore impacts), and vegetation hydraulics, subsequently testing these updates using JEDI-based snow data assimilation and retrospective coupled UFS/Noah-MP ensemble hindcasts.
Project Benefits: Improves S2S forecasting accuracy for severe early summer droughts and flood extremes in the Southern Great Plains, assists operational modelers with fixing persistent land-memory state biases, and expands public access to cross-compatible model logic and high-fidelity dataset structures through the Common Community Physics Package (CCPP) open-science repository.

Project Title: Utilizing Water Isotopic Composition in the Unified Forecast System to Constrain Precipitation and Hydrologic Processes
Project Goal: The primary goal is to guide the development and analysis of the Unified Forecast System (UFS) by integrating advanced stable water isotope (SWI) modeling and observational capabilities, focusing specifically on precipitation and hydrological processes.
Project Description: This project implements stable water isotopes in both liquid and vapor phases as an innovative hydrometeorological diagnostic within the UFS atmosphere and land models. Key research activities include creating a diagnostic hydrologic cycle for stable water isotopes within the Common Community Physics Package (CCPP) that follows standard model water without affecting the prognostic state, compiling multi-platform isotope observations from surface networks and satellite sensors into the JEDI-METplus verification system, and utilizing these tools to diagnose moist processes during Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) events and hydrological extremes like atmospheric rivers and the North American Monsoon.
Project Benefits: Provides independent observational constraints on model parameterizations using isotopic measurements, enables process-oriented evaluation of model biases by comparing modeled isotopic composition against real-world observations, and lays the groundwork for an isotope-enabled Earth prediction system and future isotope data assimilation to improve overall weather and S2S predictability.

Project Title: Enhancing NOAA UFS subseasonal to seasonal predictions of precipitation and drought via improved representation of snowpack processes
Project Goal: The primary goal is to enhance the NOAA Unified Forecast System (UFS) capabilities for subseasonal to seasonal (S2S) forecasts of precipitation and drought by improving snowpack processes and their coupling with the atmosphere, specifically focusing on snowpack-precipitation feedback.
Research Keywords: Coupled Models & Techniques, Dynamics and Nesting, Parameterization
Project Description: This project addresses significant biases in S2S snowpack modeling within the Noah-MP land component of the NOAA UFS, which currently lead to deficiencies in representing land-atmosphere interactions. Project Benefits: Produces an improved scientific understanding of snowpack-precipitation feedback loops, yields an enhanced community NOAA UFS model configuration with superior subgrid snow representation capabilities, and delivers process-oriented diagnostic feedback parameters directly to operational model teams at the Environmental Modeling Center (EMC).

Project Title: The Road to the Seasonal Forecast System: Improving Prediction of Precipitation Extremes
Project Goal: The goal of this project is to improve the prediction skill for precipitation extremes (both high and low) within the NOAA Unified Forecast System (UFS) at subseasonal to seasonal (S2S) time scales, with a focus on enhancing the reliability of these forecasts for decision-making.
Research Keywords: Data Assimilation and Ensembles, Teleconnections, Verification & Validation
Associated Forecast Systems & Models: North American Multi-Model Ensemble (NMME), Seasonal Forecast System (SFS), Unified Forecast System (UFS)
Project Description: This project focuses on evaluating and refining the UFS to better capture the physical processes that lead to precipitation extremes. Key activities include conducting a comprehensive diagnostic evaluation of the UFS performance regarding its ability to simulate the frequency, intensity, and duration of precipitation extremes over the contiguous United States, investigating the dynamical and physical mechanisms-such as atmospheric blocking, moisture transport, and soil-atmosphere feedback-that contribute to extreme precipitation events in the model, performing sensitivity experiments to understand how changes in model resolution, physics parameterizations, and initialization strategies affect the simulation of extreme events, and developing metrics and verification protocols specifically tailored to evaluate the UFS's skill in predicting extreme events rather than just mean state performance.
Project Benefits: The research will provide actionable insights into the systematic biases of the UFS, leading to improved skill in forecasting extreme precipitation events, which are high-impact phenomena for society. By providing more reliable S2S forecasts for extremes, the project supports stakeholders in water resource management, agriculture, and emergency preparedness, while providing direct feedback to the NOAA UFS development community to prioritize model improvements that specifically address weaknesses in extreme event representation and advancing the fundamental scientific understanding of the predictability of extreme precipitation at lead times of weeks to months.
